title: DART: Domain-Agnostic Residual Transfer for Generalist Anomaly Detection
claim: Baseline residual features entangle anomaly type with domain identity, while our disentanglement yields compact clusters by anomaly type with domains mixed.
layout: 2 side-by-side t-SNE panels, left-to-right, shared color/shape legends in each
description: Two side-by-side t-SNE scatter plots labeled (a) SotA and (b) DART. Points are colored by defect type (break, crack, contamination, color, print, deformation, cut, hole, scratch, surface, thread) and drawn with marker shapes for source domain (bottle, cable, capsule, carpet, and so on). Each panel has two legends at the right: Defect Type (color) at the top and Domain (shape) at the bottom. In (a), points are scattered into many small fragmented groups, with a dense overlapping blob in the center where colors mix. Same-colored points sit in several distant places and are often grouped by shape. In (b), points form about ten compact, well-separated single-color clusters, each containing many different marker shapes. The eye goes first to the clean colorful clusters on the right, in contrast with the messy left panel.
caption: t-SNE visualization of residual features before and after DART. Colors denote defect types, while marker shapes denote source domains. (a) In the SotA baseline, residuals are fragmented and strongly influenced by domain identity: samples with the same defect type appear in multiple separated regions, while different defect types often overlap. This indicates that residuals encode both anomaly information and domain-specific factors. (b) With DART, residuals form more compact and well-separated clusters by defect type, while different domains are mixed within each cluster. This shows that DART suppresses domain-specific variation and yields residual representations that are more aligned with transferable anomaly semantics.
abstract: Generalist Anomaly Detection (GAD) aims to detect anomalies in unseen domains using only a few reference samples. Recent normal-abnormal guided methods improve this setting by exploiting abnormal references, but their residuals often mix transferable anomaly cues with domain-specific appearance factors such as texture, geometry, and acquisition conditions. This residual domain entanglement limits cross-domain transfer and may produce spurious activations on novel domains. We propose DART, a plug-in framework for normal-abnormal guided GAD that learns to separate residuals into anomaly-relevant and domain-specific components. DART combines a Residual Disentanglement Module, which preserves anomaly-discriminative information while suppressing domain information, with Cross-Domain Meta-Training, which forms episodes across source domains to make the separation effective. The method is architecture-agnostic and can be inserted between residual computation and the detection head of existing GAD pipelines. Experiments on MVTec AD, VisA, and BraTS show consistent improvements over multiple base methods, with the largest gains under stronger domain shifts. https://github.com/aqeeelmirza/DART
